statement: Let $(A, \mathfrak m)$ be a complete [Noetherian local ring](c:noetherian-local-ring) whose [spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) is $k$-connected, and let $f \in \mathfrak m$. Then $\operatorname{Spec}(A/fA)$ is $(k-1)$-connected. Here a Noetherian scheme is $k$-connected if its dimension exceeds $k$ and the complement of every closed subset of dimension less than $k$ is [connected](c:connected-space).

hypotheses.text: The ring $A$ is a Noetherian [complete local ring](c:complete-local-ring) with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.
The [spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is $k$-connected.
The element $f$ lies in the [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$.

proofs.name: Local cohomology and chains of components
proofs.slogan: Reduce to complete local domains, then show that a hypersurface section of a domain cannot split, by local cohomology.
proofs.scope: Outline of the local-cohomology proof, which rests on the cited lectures for the vanishing step. The trivial cases $f = 0$ and $k \le 0$ are left out.

roles.why: Completeness makes each quotient $A/\mathfrak p$ a catenary local domain, where Hartshorne-Lichtenbaum vanishing holds.
It gives components of dimension above $k$ and chains of components with large intersections.
Because $f \in \mathfrak m$, the set $V(f)$ contains the closed point, and $fB$ is a principal ideal.

steps.slogan: Describe $k$-connectedness by chains of irreducible components.
steps.detail: A Noetherian scheme is $k$-connected exactly when every irreducible component has dimension above $k$ and any two components are joined by a chain whose consecutive members meet in dimension at least $k$. A closed set of dimension below $k$ cannot cut such a chain, and a missing chain gives a separating closed set of dimension below $k$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $V(f)$ minus a small closed set splits, and name the parts by ideals.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be a complete local domain of dimension $n \ge 2$ and $0 \ne f \in \mathfrak m_B$, and suppose $V(f) \setminus Z = Y_1 \sqcup Y_2$ with $\dim Z < n-2$ and $Y_1, Y_2$ nonempty, open and closed. Every component of $V(f)$ has dimension $n-1$ (Krull), so the closures $V(\mathfrak a), V(\mathfrak b)$ of $Y_1, Y_2$ have union $V(f)$ and $s = \dim B/(\mathfrak a + \mathfrak b) < n-2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the cohomological dimension of $\mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b$ from below.
steps.detail: The Mayer-Vietoris sequence of local cohomology links $H^i_{\mathfrak a + \mathfrak b}(B)$, $H^i_{\mathfrak a}(B) \oplus H^i_{\mathfrak b}(B)$ and $H^i_{\mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b}(B)$. With the Hartshorne-Lichtenbaum vanishing theorem the cited lectures turn it into the bound $\operatorname{cd}(\mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b) \ge n - 1 - s$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b$ with the principal ideal $fB$ to reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: The ideals $\mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b$ and $fB$ have the same radical, and local cohomology depends only on the radical, so $\operatorname{cd}(\mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b) = \operatorname{cd}(fB) \le 1$. Then $n-1-s \le 1$ gives $s \ge n-2$, against $s < n-2$. So $V(f) \setminus Z$ is connected, and $\operatorname{Spec}(B/fB)$ is $(n-2)$-connected.

steps.slogan: Glue the domain cases along the chains of components of $\operatorname{Spec} A$.
steps.detail: Let $C_i = V(\mathfrak p_i)$ be the components, of dimension $n_i \ge k+1$. By the domain case each $V(f) \cap C_i$ is $(n_i-2)$-connected, hence $(k-1)$-connected (if $f \in \mathfrak p_i$ it is $C_i$ itself). Consecutive components of a chain meet inside $V(f)$ in dimension at least $k-1$ by Krull's theorem, so the chain criterion gives $(k-1)$-connectedness; also $\dim A/fA \ge \dim A - 1 \ge k$.

concepts.c:noetherian-local-ring: Noetherian local rings carry the dimension theory and local cohomology used here.
concepts.c:complete-local-ring: Completeness gives catenary local domains and the vanishing theorem.
concepts.c:prime-spectrum: Its closed subsets and their dimensions define $k$-connectedness.
concepts.c:connected-space: The proof transfers connectedness of small complements from $\operatorname{Spec} A$ to $V(f)$.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: The element $f$ in $\mathfrak m$ makes $V(f)$ contain the closed point.

source.ref: C. Huneke, Lectures on local cohomology (with an appendix by Amelia Taylor), in: Interactions between Homotopy Theory and Algebra, Contemporary Mathematics 436, American Mathematical Society, 2007, 51-99
source.note: The lectures aim at Grothendieck's connectedness theorem (SGA 2, Expose XIII, Theoreme 2.1). The estimate of step 3 and its use of Hartshorne-Lichtenbaum vanishing are in the lectures.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field), $m \ge 1$, $S$ a finite set of primes of $K$, and $x \in K$ an $m$-th power in the [completion](c:completion) $K_v$ for every prime $v \notin S$. Then $x \in K^m$, except in the special case of the scope, where $x \in K^m \cup (2+\eta_s)^{m/2} K^m$.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field), $m \ge 1$ is an integer, and $S$ is a finite set of primes of $K$.
The element $x \in K$ is an $m$-th power in $K_v$ for every prime $v \notin S$.

conclusion: The element $x$ is an $m$-th power in $K$, except in the special case, where $x \in K^m \cup (2+\eta_s)^{m/2} K^m$.

proofs.name: Kummer classes and Chebotarev
proofs.slogan: Read $x$ as a locally trivial Kummer class, pass to the cyclotomic field, and compute a cohomology group on cyclic subgroups.
proofs.scope: Special means: for $s$ maximal with $\eta_s = \zeta_{2^s} + \zeta_{2^s}^{-1} \in K$, the numbers $-1$, $2+\eta_s$, $-(2+\eta_s)$ are non-squares in $K$, $2^{s+1} \mid m$, and $S$ holds every $v \mid 2$ where all three are non-squares in $K_v$. The proof is an outline that rests on the cited cohomological computation.

roles.why: A [number field](c:number-field) has Chebotarev's theorem, and the finite set $S$ leaves almost all primes in play.
The local power condition makes the Kummer class of $x$ vanish at almost all primes.

steps.slogan: Read the hypothesis as a Kummer class that vanishes at almost all primes.
steps.detail: The class of $x$ in $K^\times / K^{\times m} = H^1(K, \mu_m)$, a [Galois cohomology](c:galois-cohomology) group, restricts to zero in $H^1(K_v, \mu_m)$ for every $v \notin S$. So $x$ gives an element of the group $\text{Ш}^1(K, S)$ of such classes, and the claim says that this group is trivial outside the special case.

steps.slogan: Pass to the [cyclotomic](c:cyclotomic-field) extension $L = K(\mu_m)$ and apply Chebotarev.
steps.detail: Over $L$ the Kummer extension $L(x^{1/m})/L$ is cyclic, and almost all primes of $L$ split completely in it. By Chebotarev's density theorem it is trivial, so $x \in L^m$. By inflation-restriction, $\text{Ш}^1(K, S)$ embeds in $H^1(G, \mu_m(L))$ with $G = \operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$.

steps.slogan: Restrict the class to every cyclic subgroup of $G$.
steps.detail: By Chebotarev every cyclic subgroup $C \subseteq G$ is the decomposition group of a prime $v \notin S$, and the local condition kills the class in $H^1(C, \mu_m)$. So the class lies in the subgroup of $H^1(G, \mu_m)$ that vanishes on all cyclic subgroups.

steps.slogan: Compute which classes vanish on all cyclic subgroups of $G$.
steps.detail: The cited work computes this subgroup for $G \subseteq (\mathbb Z/m)^\times$ acting on the cyclic group $\mu_m$. It is zero except in a case that involves only the $2$-part of $G$; there it has order $2$, and the cited work identifies the nonzero class with $(2+\eta_s)^{m/2}$.

steps.slogan: Add the condition on the primes above $2$ that lie in $S$.
steps.detail: In the exceptional case the class is locally trivial at a prime $v \mid 2$ with $v \notin S$ only if one of the three numbers is a square in $K_v$, because otherwise the decomposition group at $v$ is not cyclic and the class survives there. This gives the condition on $S$ in the special case.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $x$ is an $m$-th power in $K$ outside the special case.
steps.detail: If $(K, m, S)$ is not special, the group $\text{Ш}^1(K, S)$ is zero, so $x \in K^m$. In the special case it has order $2$, so $x \in K^m \cup (2+\eta_s)^{m/2} K^m$.

concepts.c:number-field: The theorem is about elements of a number field and its primes.
concepts.c:completion: The hypothesis is a condition in each completion $K_v$.
concepts.c:galois-cohomology: The Kummer class and its local restrictions live in Galois cohomology.
concepts.c:cyclotomic-field: Adjoining $\mu_m$ makes Kummer theory over $L$ cyclic.

source.ref: E. Artin and J. Tate, Class Field Theory, Chapter X (The Grunwald-Wang theorem), W. A. Benjamin, 1967; reprinted by AMS Chelsea Publishing, 2009
source.note: Wang corrected Grunwald's claim; the example $16 \in \mathbb Q$, $m = 8$, $S = \{2\}$ is special. The cohomological reading of steps 2 to 5 is the one used in the cited chapter.

statement: Let $d \ge 1$ and let $T_1, \dots, T_d$ be finitely branching [trees](c:tree) of height $\omega$ without terminal nodes. For every finite coloring of the level product $\bigcup_n T_1(n) \times \dots \times T_d(n)$ there are [strong subtrees](c:strong-subtree) $S_i \subseteq T_i$ with a common level set whose level product is monochromatic.

hypotheses.text: The [trees](c:tree) $T_1, \dots, T_d$ are finitely branching, have height $\omega$, and have no terminal nodes.
The level product $\bigcup_n T_1(n) \times \dots \times T_d(n)$ is colored with finitely many colors.

conclusion: There are [strong subtrees](c:strong-subtree) $S_i \subseteq T_i$ with the same level set such that the level product of the $S_i$ has one color.

proofs.name: Harrington's forcing proof
proofs.slogan: Reduce to two colors, recast the claim for dense sets, and find homogeneous conditions by forcing and a partition relation.
proofs.scope: Outline of Harrington's proof for finitely branching trees; steps 2 to 4 rest on the cited work. Other members of the family are the dense-set version for infinitely branching trees and Milliken's theorem for one tree.

roles.why: The finite branching and the missing terminal nodes let the forcing and the homogeneous conditions define [strong subtrees](c:strong-subtree).
The finite number of colors lets the proof peel off one color class at a time.

steps.slogan: Reduce the finite coloring to a dichotomy for one set of level tuples.
steps.detail: It is enough to show that for every set $X$ of level tuples some strong subtrees with a common level set have their level product inside $X$ or inside its complement. Apply this to one color class, then to the other colors inside the new subtrees, at most $r-1$ times; strong subtrees of strong subtrees are strong subtrees.

steps.slogan: Recast the dichotomy as a statement about dense sets of level tuples.
steps.detail: The cited proofs turn the dichotomy for $X$ into the dense-set form of the theorem, in which a set of level tuples that is dense above every node must contain a level product of strong subtrees. This form is the one that the forcing argument handles.

steps.slogan: Force with finite approximations and read the combinatorics of trees as combinatorics of cardinals.
steps.detail: Harrington's argument uses a forcing poset of finite approximations to $d$ generic branches, but it never leaves the ground model. The forcing relation transfers the Ramsey-theoretic claim about the trees to a Ramsey-theoretic claim about cardinals.

steps.slogan: Apply a partition relation for cardinals to get homogeneous conditions.
steps.detail: A cardinal $\kappa$ with a partition relation $\kappa \to (\aleph_0)^{2d}$ of Erdos-Rado type gives an infinite set of conditions that behave alike. Their common behavior fixes the levels and the nodes of the subtrees.

steps.slogan: Extract the strong subtrees and repeat over the colors.
steps.detail: Reading the homogeneous conditions as levels and nodes gives strong subtrees $S_1, \dots, S_d$ with a common level set whose level product meets the dense set. Step 1 then yields a monochromatic level product for the given coloring.

concepts.c:tree: The theorem concerns level products of trees.
concepts.c:strong-subtree: Strong subtrees are the objects the proof produces and keep branching.

source.ref: I. Farah and S. Todorcevic, Some applications of the method of forcing, Yenisei, Moscow, 1995 (Harrington's forcing proof); S. Todorcevic, Introduction to Ramsey Spaces, Annals of Mathematics Studies 174, Princeton University Press, 2010; original: J. D. Halpern and H. Lauchli, A partition theorem, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 124 (1966), 360-367
source.note: Steps 2 to 4 follow Harrington's proof as presented by Farah and Todorcevic; the details of the forcing and of the partition relation are in the cited texts.

statement: Let $K/\mathbb Q$ be a finite [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension) with group $G$. Then the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal O_K$ has a [normal integral basis](c:normal-integral-basis), a $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{\sigma(\alpha) : \sigma \in G\}$, if and only if $K$ is tamely ramified at every prime.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a finite [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension) of $\mathbb Q$ with Galois group $G$.

conclusion: $\mathcal O_K$ has a normal integral basis if and only if the [ramification index](c:ramification-index) of every prime $p$ in $K$ is prime to $p$.

proofs.name: Cyclotomic basis and trace
proofs.slogan: Tame fields sit in squarefree cyclotomic fields that have a basis of roots of unity, and a basis forces the local trace to be onto.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem: steps 1 to 3 prove that tame ramification gives a basis, and steps 4 and 5 prove the converse. Tame means that every ramification index is prime to its residue characteristic.

roles.why: Abelian means $K \subseteq \mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$ by Kronecker-Weber, and all inertia groups above $p$ coincide.

steps.slogan: Show that a tame abelian field lies in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$ with $m$ odd and squarefree.
steps.detail: By Kronecker-Weber take $m$ least with $K \subseteq \mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$ and let $H = \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)/K)$. If $p^2 \mid m$, the kernel $N_p$ of $(\mathbb Z/p^a)^\times \to (\mathbb Z/p^{a-1})^\times$ has order $p$ and is not in $H$ by minimality, so $p \mid e_p(K)$. If $2 \parallel m$, then $\mathbb Q(\zeta_m) = \mathbb Q(\zeta_{m/2})$, against minimality.

steps.slogan: Give $\mathbb Z[\zeta_m]$ the basis $\{\zeta_m^a\}$ of conjugates of $\zeta_m$.
steps.detail: For a prime $p$, the elements $\zeta_p, \dots, \zeta_p^{p-1}$ form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\mathbb Z[\zeta_p]$, since $1 = -\sum_{a \ge 1} \zeta_p^a$ and the change of basis from $1, \dots, \zeta_p^{p-2}$ is unimodular. For squarefree $m$, $\mathbb Z[\zeta_m] = \bigotimes_{p \mid m} \mathbb Z[\zeta_p]$, and the product basis is $\{\zeta_m^a : a \in (\mathbb Z/m)^\times\}$.

steps.slogan: Descend the basis to $K$ by summing over the cosets of $H$.
steps.detail: The group $H$ acts freely on the basis $\{\sigma \zeta_m\}$, so $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[\zeta_m]^H$ has the orbit sums $\beta_{\sigma H} = \sum_{h \in H} h \sigma \zeta_m$ as a $\mathbb Z$-basis. As $G$ is abelian, $\beta_{\sigma H} = \sigma(\beta_H)$, so the conjugates of $\beta_H = \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)/K}(\zeta_m)$ form a normal integral basis.

steps.slogan: Turn a normal integral basis into a surjective local trace to the inertia field.
steps.detail: If $\mathcal O_K = \bigoplus_\sigma \mathbb Z\,\sigma(\alpha)$, then $\mathcal O_K \otimes \mathbb Z_p$ is free over $\mathbb Z_p[G]$, hence over $\mathbb Z_p[I]$, where $I$ is the inertia group above $p$ (the same for all primes above $p$). A free $\mathbb Z_p[I]$-module $M$ has $M^I = (\sum_{\tau \in I} \tau) M$, so the trace $\mathcal O_K \otimes \mathbb Z_p \to \mathcal O_L \otimes \mathbb Z_p$ is onto, with $L = K^I$.

steps.slogan: Show that the local trace is not onto when $p$ divides the ramification index.
steps.detail: At a prime $\mathfrak P \mid p$ of $K$, the extension $K_{\mathfrak P}/L_{\mathfrak q}$ is totally ramified of degree $e = |I|$, and $\mathfrak P$ is the only prime above $\mathfrak q$. If $p \mid e$ the different has exponent $d \ge e$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal O_{K_{\mathfrak P}}) = \mathfrak q^{\lfloor d/e \rfloor} \subseteq \mathfrak q$, which contradicts surjectivity. So $p \nmid e$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 show that a tamely ramified $K$ has a normal integral basis. Steps 4 and 5 show that a field with a normal integral basis has ramification index prime to $p$ at every prime $p$, so it is tamely ramified.

concepts.c:abelian-extension: Abelian extensions of $\mathbb Q$ are subfields of cyclotomic fields.
concepts.c:ring-of-integers: The basis question is about the $\mathbb Z$-module $\mathcal O_K$.
concepts.c:normal-integral-basis: This is the object whose existence the theorem decides.
concepts.c:ramification-index: Tameness is the condition that $e$ is prime to $p$.

source.note: Hilbert's Zahlbericht treats cyclotomic fields and Speiser extends the result to abelian fields; the converse is Noether's trace argument, written locally here.

statement: Let $\Gamma \subseteq \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ be a [congruence subgroup](c:congruence-subgroup), $X_\Gamma$ its [modular curve](c:modular-curve), and $c_1, c_2$ two [cusps](c:cusp) of $X_\Gamma$. Then the class of the divisor $c_1 - c_2$ in the [Jacobian variety](c:jacobian-variety) of $X_\Gamma$ has finite order.

hypotheses.text: The group $\Gamma$ is a [congruence subgroup](c:congruence-subgroup) of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, so $\Gamma \supseteq \Gamma(N)$ for some $N$.
The points $c_1$ and $c_2$ are [cusps](c:cusp) of the [modular curve](c:modular-curve) $X_\Gamma$.

conclusion: The class of $c_1 - c_2$ in the [Jacobian variety](c:jacobian-variety) $J(X_\Gamma)$ is a torsion point.

proofs.name: Hecke operators and the Weil bound
proofs.slogan: A Hecke operator acts on cuspidal divisors with large eigenvalues and on the Jacobian with eigenvalues below the Weil bound, so it separates them.
proofs.scope: Outline of the Manin-Drinfeld argument; the computation of the action on cusps and the Eichler-Shimura relation rest on the cited papers. The case of the full modular group is trivial because it has one cusp.

roles.why: A [congruence subgroup](c:congruence-subgroup) contains $\Gamma(N)$, which reduces the claim to $X(N)$ and gives Hecke operators.
The difference of two [cusps](c:cusp) is a degree-zero cuspidal divisor on which Hecke operators act.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to degree-zero cuspidal divisors on $X(N)$.
steps.detail: Choose $N$ with $\Gamma(N) \subseteq \Gamma$. The map $\pi\colon X(N) \to X_\Gamma$ has some degree $d$, and $\pi_* \pi^* = d$ on Jacobians, so $\pi^*$ has finite kernel. The pullback of $c_1 - c_2$ is a degree-zero cuspidal divisor on $X(N)$, so it is enough to show that such divisors have finite order.

steps.slogan: Compute the action of a Hecke operator $T_\ell$ on degree-zero cuspidal divisors.
steps.detail: Choose a prime $\ell \equiv 1 \pmod N$ with $\ell \ge 7$. The cited papers show that on cusps $T_\ell = \ell \sigma_1 + \sigma_2$ for commuting permutations $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$ of the cusps, so every eigenvalue of $T_\ell$ on the lattice of degree-zero cuspidal divisors has absolute value at least $\ell - 1$.

steps.slogan: Bound the eigenvalues of $T_\ell$ on the Jacobian by $2\sqrt{\ell}$.
steps.detail: For $\ell \equiv 1 \pmod N$ the Eichler-Shimura relation writes $T_\ell$ as Frobenius plus Verschiebung on the reduction of $X(N)$ at $\ell$. The Weil bound for curves over finite fields gives all eigenvalues of $T_\ell$ on $J(X(N)) \otimes \mathbb Q$ absolute value at most $2\sqrt{\ell}$.

steps.slogan: Kill a cuspidal divisor by the characteristic polynomial of $T_\ell$.
steps.detail: Let $P$ be the characteristic polynomial of $T_\ell$ on the free group of degree-zero cuspidal divisors. By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem $P(T_\ell) D = 0$ for each such divisor $D$. The class map to the Jacobian commutes with $T_\ell$, so $P(T_\ell)[D] = 0$ in $J(X(N)) \otimes \mathbb Q$.

steps.slogan: Invert $P(T_\ell)$ on the Jacobian to show that the class is torsion.
steps.detail: Every root of $P$ has absolute value at least $\ell - 1 > 2\sqrt{\ell}$ for $\ell \ge 7$, so no root is an eigenvalue of $T_\ell$ on $J \otimes \mathbb Q$. Hence $P(T_\ell)$ is invertible there and $[D] = 0$ in $J \otimes \mathbb Q$, so $[D]$ has finite order; step 1 transfers this to $c_1 - c_2$ on $X_\Gamma$.

concepts.c:congruence-subgroup: It contains a principal congruence subgroup, which reduces the problem to full level.
concepts.c:modular-curve: The Hecke operators and the Weil bound act on this curve and its Jacobian.
concepts.c:cusp: The divisors in question are supported on the cusps.
concepts.c:jacobian-variety: Finite order is a statement about a point of the Jacobian.

source.ref: Yu. I. Manin, Parabolic points and zeta functions of modular forms, Izvestiya Akademii Nauk SSSR, Seriya Matematicheskaya 36 (1972), 19-66; V. G. Drinfeld, Two theorems on modular curves, Functional Analysis and Its Applications 7 (1973), 155-156
source.note: Manin proved the case of the groups $\Gamma_0(N)$ and Drinfeld the general congruence case; both use Hecke operators with the Weil bound.

statement: Let $S$ be a nonsingular projective complex surface with a morphism $\varphi\colon S \to \mathbb P^1$ whose general fibre is a [projective line](c:projective-line), so that the fibres form a [pencil of rational curves](c:pencil-of-rational-curves). Then $S$ is a [rational surface](c:rational-surface): it is [birational](c:birational-map) to $\mathbb P^2$.

hypotheses.text: $S$ is a nonsingular projective algebraic surface over $\mathbb C$.
There is a morphism $\varphi\colon S \to \mathbb P^1$ whose general fibre is isomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$, a [pencil of rational curves](c:pencil-of-rational-curves).

conclusion: The surface $S$ is birational to $\mathbb P^2$.

proofs.name: Generic fibre and Tsen's theorem
proofs.slogan: The generic fibre is a conic over $\mathbb C(t)$, Tsen's theorem gives it a rational point, and then it is a line over $\mathbb C(t)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $S$ over $\mathbb C$; singular fibres play no role because only the generic fibre is used. The same argument works over any algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$.

roles.why: Integrality of $S$ makes $\mathbb C(S)$ the function field of the generic fibre over $\mathbb C(t)$.
The general fibre $\mathbb P^1$ makes the generic fibre a smooth curve of genus $0$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the generic fibre as a curve over $K = \mathbb C(t)$.
steps.detail: The generic fibre $C$ of $\varphi$ is a projective curve over $K = \mathbb C(t)$ whose [function field](c:function-field) is $\mathbb C(S)$. Because the general fibre is $\mathbb P^1$, generic smoothness in characteristic $0$ shows that $C$ is smooth, geometrically integral and of genus $0$.

steps.slogan: Embed the genus-zero curve $C$ as a plane conic over $K$.
steps.detail: The anticanonical bundle $\omega_C^{-1}$ is defined over $K$ and has degree $2$. By Riemann-Roch $h^0 = 3$, and it is very ample because it becomes $\mathcal O(2)$ over $\bar K$, so it embeds $C$ as a conic in $\mathbb P^2_K$.

steps.slogan: Find a $K$-rational point on the conic by Tsen's theorem.
steps.detail: The field $K = \mathbb C(t)$ is [quasi-algebraically closed](c:quasi-algebraically-closed-field) by Tsen's theorem: a form of degree $d$ in more than $d$ variables has a nontrivial zero. The conic is a quadratic form in $3$ variables, so $C(K) \ne \emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Project the conic from its rational point to identify $C$ with $\mathbb P^1_K$.
steps.detail: Projection from a $K$-point $P$ of a smooth conic sends each line through $P$ to its second intersection point with the conic, which is rational over $K$. This is an isomorphism $C \cong \mathbb P^1_K$, so $K(C) = K(u)$ is purely transcendental.

steps.slogan: Read off $\mathbb C(S) = \mathbb C(t, u)$ and conclude that $S$ is rational.
steps.detail: Then $\mathbb C(S) = K(C) = \mathbb C(t)(u) = \mathbb C(t, u)$, a purely transcendental extension of $\mathbb C$ of degree $2$. This is the function field of $\mathbb P^2$, so $S$ is birational to $\mathbb P^2$.

concepts.c:projective-line: The general fibre is a projective line.
concepts.c:pencil-of-rational-curves: The fibres of $\varphi$ form the pencil whose generic member is studied.
concepts.c:birational-map: Rationality means a birational map to the plane.
concepts.c:function-field: The proof compares the function field of $S$ with that of its generic fibre.
concepts.c:quasi-algebraically-closed-field: Tsen's theorem makes $\mathbb C(t)$ quasi-algebraically closed, which gives the point.

source.note: This is the classical argument of Noether, Enriques and Tsen; see Beauville, Complex Algebraic Surfaces, Chapter III.

statement: Let $K$ be a strict [2-category](c:2-category). The quintet construction $Q(K)$ has the objects of $K$, the 1-cells as horizontal and vertical arrows, and as squares with top $h$, bottom $k$, left $v$ and right $w$ the 2-cells $kv \Rightarrow wh$. With pasting as composition, $Q(K)$ is a [double category](c:double-category).

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a strict [2-category](c:2-category).

conclusion: $Q(K)$ is a [double category](c:double-category): both compositions of squares are associative and unital, and they satisfy the [interchange law](c:interchange-law).

proofs.name: Pasting of squares
proofs.slogan: Define both compositions of squares by whiskering and vertical composition of 2-cells, and check the laws in the 2-category.
proofs.scope: The whole construction, with the convention that a square is a 2-cell $kv \Rightarrow wh$; the opposite convention gives an isomorphic double category. For a bicategory the same argument works after inserting the coherence isomorphisms.

roles.why: The strict associativity of 1-cells, the functoriality of whiskering and the [interchange law](c:interchange-law) of $K$ give every law of $Q(K)$.

steps.slogan: Define the squares and the two kinds of identity squares.
steps.detail: A square is a 2-cell $\alpha\colon kv \Rightarrow wh$ in $K$. The horizontal identity of a vertical arrow $v$ has top $1_A$, bottom $1_C$ and sides $v$, and it is the identity 2-cell $1_v$. The vertical identity of a horizontal arrow $h$ is $1_h$ in the same way.

steps.slogan: Define [horizontal composition](c:horizontal-composition) of squares by whiskering and vertical composition of 2-cells.
steps.detail: For $\alpha\colon kv \Rightarrow wh$ and $\beta\colon k'w \Rightarrow xh'$ set $\alpha \mid \beta = (\beta h) \cdot (k' \alpha)$. This is a 2-cell $k'kv \Rightarrow xh'h$, so a square with top $h'h$, bottom $k'k$, left $v$ and right $x$.

steps.slogan: Define [vertical composition](c:vertical-composition) of squares in the same way.
steps.detail: For $\alpha\colon kv \Rightarrow wh$ and $\gamma\colon m v' \Rightarrow w'k$ set $\gamma / \alpha = (w' \alpha) \cdot (\gamma v)$. This is a 2-cell $m v' v \Rightarrow w' w h$, so a square with top $h$, bottom $m$, left $v'v$ and right $w'w$.

steps.slogan: Check associativity and the unit laws from functoriality of whiskering.
steps.detail: Whiskering is functorial: $(\beta \cdot \alpha) h = \beta h \cdot \alpha h$ and $k'(\beta \cdot \alpha) = k' \beta \cdot k' \alpha$. Expanding both bracketings of three squares gives $(\delta h'h)(k''\beta h)(k''k'\alpha)$, so horizontal composition is associative; the vertical case is the mirror image. Composing with an identity square whiskers by identities, which changes nothing.

steps.slogan: Prove the interchange law for squares from the [interchange law](c:interchange-law) of 2-cells.
steps.detail: For a $2 \times 2$ grid of squares, both orders of composition expand to the same composite of four whiskered 2-cells. Two 2-cells that act on separate sides commute by the interchange law of $K$, which identifies the two expansions.

steps.slogan: Assemble the data and the laws into a double category.
steps.detail: A double category has objects, horizontal and vertical categories, squares with two compositions and identities, and the interchange law. Steps 1 to 5 supply them, and the horizontal and vertical categories are both the 1-category underlying $K$.

concepts.c:2-category: Its 1-cells and 2-cells supply the arrows and squares.
concepts.c:double-category: The construction is checked to satisfy the axioms of a double category.
concepts.c:interchange-law: The interchange law of 2-cells becomes the interchange law of squares.
concepts.c:horizontal-composition: It glues two squares that share a vertical side.
concepts.c:vertical-composition: It glues two squares that share a horizontal side.

source.note: Ehresmann's quintets; the squares and the pasting formulas follow the nLab entry on the quintet construction.

statement: Let $s$ be a finite subset of a [normed field](c:normed-field) $\mathbb K$ and let $\log^+ t = \max(0, \log t)$. There is a constant $C$ such that $\sum_{a \in s} \log^+ \frac{1}{|w - a|} \le \log^+ \Bigl|\sum_{a \in s} \frac{1}{w - a}\Bigr| + C$ for every $w \in \mathbb K \setminus s$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathbb K$ is a [normed field](c:normed-field).
$s \subseteq \mathbb K$ is a finite set.

conclusion: There is a constant $C$ such that the inequality of the statement holds for every $w \in \mathbb K \setminus s$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for every $w \in \mathbb K$ with the convention $0^{-1} = 0$, so the terms with $w \in s$ are $0$ on the left. This statement keeps $w \notin s$ because $\sum 1/(w-a)$ needs it.

proofs.name: Gap and case split
proofs.slogan: Take a gap $\delta$ between the points and split into $w$ far from $s$ and $w$ close to one point.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The sets with at most one point are trivial, and the case split uses the minimal gap $\delta$ of $s$.

roles.why: The triangle inequality of the [norm](c:normed-field) keeps $w$ away from the other points of $s$.
Finiteness gives a positive minimal gap and a finite number of terms in every bound.

steps.slogan: Treat the sets with at most one point directly.
steps.detail: If $s = \emptyset$, both sides are $0$ and $C = 0$ works. If $s = \{a\}$, the left side is $\log^+ \frac{1}{|w-a|}$ and the right side is $\log^+ \frac{1}{|w-a|} + C$, so $C = 0$ works again.

steps.slogan: Choose the gap $\delta$ and the constant $C$ for $q = |s| \ge 2$.
steps.detail: Let $\delta = \min(1, \min_{a \ne b} |a - b|)$, which is positive because $s$ is finite. Put $C = q \log^+ \frac{2q}{\delta} + \log q$, which is nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Bound the left side when $w$ is far from every point of $s$.
steps.detail: If $|w - a| \ge \frac{\delta}{2q}$ for all $a \in s$, then each term is at most $\log^+ \frac{2q}{\delta}$. So the left side is at most $q \log^+ \frac{2q}{\delta} \le C$, and the right side is at least $C$ because $\log^+ \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the terms of the other points when $w$ is close to one point $a_0$.
steps.detail:
Suppose $|w - a_0| <  rac{\delta}{2q}$. For $b 
e a_0$ the triangle inequality gives $|w - b| \ge |a_0 - b| - |w - a_0| \ge \delta -  rac{\delta}{4} \ge  rac{\delta}{2}$. Hence $\sum_{b 
e a_0} \log^+  rac{1}{|w-b|} \le (q-1) \log^+  rac{2q}{\delta}$ and $ igl|\sum_{b 
e a_0}  rac{1}{w-b} igr| \le  rac{2(q-1)}{\delta}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the nearest term is controlled by the whole sum.
steps.detail: Let $t = |w - a_0|^{-1} \ge \frac{2q}{\delta}$. The tail bound gives $\bigl|\sum_{a} \frac{1}{w-a}\bigr| \ge t - \frac{2(q-1)}{\delta} \ge \frac{t}{q}$, so $t \le q \bigl|\sum_a \frac{1}{w-a}\bigr|$. Since $\log^+(qx) \le \log q + \log^+ x$, we get $\log^+ t \le \log q + \log^+ \bigl|\sum_a \frac{1}{w-a}\bigr|$.

steps.slogan: Add the head and tail bounds to get the inequality near $a_0$.
steps.detail: Near $a_0$ the left side is at most $\log q + \log^+ \bigl|\sum_a \frac{1}{w-a}\bigr| + (q-1) \log^+ \frac{2q}{\delta}$, which is at most $\log^+ \bigl|\sum_a \frac{1}{w-a}\bigr| + C$. With the far case and the case $|s| \le 1$, the inequality holds for every $w \notin s$.

concepts.c:normed-field: The proof uses only the absolute value and its triangle inequality.
concepts.c:logarithm: The positive part of the logarithm measures how close $w$ is to a point.

source.note: mathlib follows this case split, with the gap $\delta$ from infsep, the lemmas sum_posLog_inv_norm_sub_le for the far case and posLog_nat_mul for the head term.

statement: Let $X$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold), $E \subset X$ a closed complete [pluripolar set](c:pluripolar-set), and $\Theta$ a [closed positive current](c:closed-positive-current) on $X \setminus E$ whose coefficients have locally finite mass near $E$. Then the extension $\tilde\Theta$ of $\Theta$ by zero across $E$ is a closed positive current on $X$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a complex manifold, and $E \subset X$ is closed and complete [pluripolar](c:pluripolar-set): locally $E = \{u = -\infty\}$ for a plurisubharmonic $u$.
$\Theta$ is a [closed positive current](c:closed-positive-current) on $X \setminus E$.
The coefficients of $\Theta$ are measures of locally finite mass near every point of $E$.

conclusion: The trivial extension $\tilde\Theta$, obtained by extending the coefficient measures by $0$ on $E$, is a closed positive current on $X$.

proofs.name: Cutoff along the pole set
proofs.slogan: Cut $\Theta$ off near $E$ by functions of a plurisubharmonic function and show that the boundary terms vanish in the limit.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof of El Mir and Skoda as presented by Demailly; the estimate of the boundary terms in step 5 rests on the cited work. The bidimension $(p, p)$ of $\Theta$ is fixed throughout.

roles.why: The [pluripolar](c:pluripolar-set) structure gives the plurisubharmonic function whose pole set is $E$, which defines the cutoffs.
Closedness gives $d(\theta \Theta) = d\theta \wedge \Theta$, and positivity gives the Cauchy-Schwarz estimate.
Finite mass makes the extension by zero well defined and makes the cutoffs converge weakly.

steps.slogan: Extend the coefficient measures by zero and check positivity.
steps.detail: Because $\Theta$ has locally finite mass near $E$, its coefficients are Radon measures near $E$, and extending them by $0$ on $E$ defines a current $\tilde\Theta$ on $X$. It is positive, since positivity is a pointwise condition on the measures, and it is closed on $X \setminus E$.

steps.slogan: Localize and write $E$ as the pole set of a plurisubharmonic function.
steps.detail: Closedness of $\tilde\Theta$ is a local property. Near a point of $E$ choose an open set $\Omega$ and a plurisubharmonic function $u \le 0$ on $\Omega$ with $E \cap \Omega = \{u = -\infty\}$.

steps.slogan: Cut $\Theta$ off near $E$ by smooth functions of $u$.
steps.detail: Choose smooth functions $\theta_k = \chi_k \circ u$ with values in $[0, 1]$, vanishing near $E$ and increasing to $1$ on $\Omega \setminus E$. Then $\theta_k \Theta$ stays away from $E$ and converges weakly to $\tilde\Theta$ by dominated convergence.

steps.slogan: Reduce closedness to the vanishing of boundary terms.
steps.detail: Since $\Theta$ is closed on $\Omega \setminus E$, we have $d(\theta_k \Theta) = d\theta_k \wedge \Theta$ there. As $d\tilde\Theta = \lim d(\theta_k \Theta)$ weakly, it suffices to show that $d\theta_k \wedge \Theta \to 0$ weakly on $\Omega$.

steps.slogan: Show that the boundary terms tend to zero by a Cauchy-Schwarz estimate.
steps.detail: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for positive currents bounds $|\int d\theta_k \wedge \Theta \wedge \alpha|^2$ by a product of two integrals against $\Theta$. The cited proof bounds the factor with derivatives of $\theta_k$ by integrating by parts with the help of the plurisubharmonicity of $u$, and shows that it tends to $0$ because the mass of $\Theta$ near $E$ is finite.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the weak limit $\tilde\Theta$ is closed.
steps.detail: For a test form $\alpha$ we get $\langle d\tilde\Theta, \alpha \rangle = \lim \langle d\theta_k \wedge \Theta, \alpha \rangle = 0$, so $\tilde\Theta$ is closed on $\Omega$, hence on $X$. With step 1 it is a closed positive current.

concepts.c:complex-manifold: The statement lives on a complex manifold with plurisubharmonic functions.
concepts.c:pluripolar-set: The set $E$ is the pole set of a plurisubharmonic function, which defines the cutoffs.
concepts.c:closed-positive-current: The current $\Theta$ is the object that the proof extends.

source.ref: J.-P. Demailly, Analytic Methods in Algebraic Geometry, Surveys of Modern Mathematics 1, International Press and Higher Education Press, 2012
source.note: Demailly states and proves the extension theorem; the original proofs are by H. Skoda (Inventiones Mathematicae 1982) and H. El Mir (Acta Mathematica 1984).

statement: Let $C$ and $C'$ be non-singular projective [algebraic curves](c:algebraic-curve) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, both of [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) $g > 1$. Then every nonconstant rational map $C \dashrightarrow C'$ is a [birational map](c:birational-map), and so an isomorphism.

hypotheses.text: $C$ and $C'$ are non-singular projective [algebraic curves](c:algebraic-curve) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$.
Both curves have the same [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) $g > 1$.
$\varphi\colon C \dashrightarrow C'$ is a nonconstant rational map.

conclusion: The map $\varphi$ is [birational](c:birational-map), and it is an isomorphism $C \to C'$.

proofs.name: Riemann-Hurwitz
proofs.slogan: A map of degree $d$ between curves of equal genus $g > 1$ forces $d = 1$ by the Riemann-Hurwitz formula.
proofs.scope: A rational correspondence is read as a nonconstant rational map. Characteristic $0$ is needed, since Frobenius is a non-birational map between curves of equal genus in characteristic $p$.

roles.why: Smoothness extends the rational map to a morphism, and characteristic $0$ makes it separable.
Equal [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) $g > 1$ makes $2g - 2$ positive and equal on both sides.
A nonconstant map is finite and surjective of some degree $d \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Extend the rational map to a finite morphism of degree $d$.
steps.detail: A rational map from a non-singular projective curve extends to a morphism $\varphi\colon C \to C'$, because each local ring of $C$ is a discrete valuation ring. A nonconstant morphism of projective curves is finite and surjective of degree $d = [k(C) : k(C')] \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Write the Riemann-Hurwitz formula for the morphism.
steps.detail: In characteristic $0$ the finite morphism $\varphi$ is separable, so $2g(C) - 2 = d\,(2g(C') - 2) + \deg R$, where $R \ge 0$ is the [ramification](c:branched-cover) divisor.

steps.slogan: Insert the equal genera to bound the degree $d$.
steps.detail: With $g(C) = g(C') = g$, the formula gives $2g - 2 = d(2g - 2) + \deg R \ge d(2g - 2)$. Since $2g - 2 > 0$, this gives $d \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\varphi$ has degree $1$ and is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: A morphism of degree $d = 1$ gives $k(C) = k(C')$ through $\varphi^*$, so $\varphi$ is birational. Two non-singular projective curves with the same function field are isomorphic, so $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: The theorem is about non-singular projective curves.
concepts.c:genus-of-a-surface: The genus enters the Riemann-Hurwitz formula.
concepts.c:branched-cover: A finite map of curves is a branched cover with ramification divisor $R$.

source.note: Standard consequence of Hurwitz's theorem; see Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Chapter IV, Section 2.

statement: The functor $X \mapsto C(X)$ is a dual equivalence from [compact Hausdorff spaces](c:compact-hausdorff-space) and continuous maps to uniformly complete Archimedean [Riesz spaces](c:riesz-space) with strong unit and unit-preserving Riesz homomorphisms. Its inverse sends $(E, u)$ to the space of unital Riesz homomorphisms $E \to \mathbb R$ with the weak-star topology.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ are [compact Hausdorff spaces](c:compact-hausdorff-space) and the morphisms are continuous maps.
The pairs $(E, u)$ are Archimedean [Riesz spaces](c:riesz-space) with strong unit $u$ that are complete for the unit norm $\|x\| = \inf\{\lambda : |x| \le \lambda u\}$.

conclusion: $C$ is fully faithful and every $(E, u)$ is isomorphic to $C(X_E)$, where $X_E$ is the space of unital Riesz homomorphisms $E \to \mathbb R$, so $C$ is a dual equivalence.

proofs.name: Spectrum of unital Riesz homomorphisms
proofs.slogan: Show that $C$ is fully faithful through characters, and that every unital Archimedean complete space is $C$ of its spectrum by Stone-Weierstrass.
proofs.scope: The functor, its inverse on objects and the isomorphisms; the empty space corresponds to the zero space, and the steps assume $X \ne \emptyset$ and $u \ne 0$. This is the Riesz-space analogue of Gelfand duality.

roles.why: Compactness and the Hausdorff property give point-separating continuous functions, and a finite subcover in the character step.
The Archimedean property gives enough Riesz homomorphisms, and completeness of the unit norm makes the image all of $C(X_E)$.

steps.slogan: Show that unital Riesz homomorphisms $C(X) \to \mathbb R$ are point evaluations.
steps.detail: Let $\psi$ be one. It is positive, and $g \in \ker\psi$ gives $|g| \in \ker\psi$. If no point $x$ has $f(x) = 0$ for all $f \in \ker\psi$, a finite subcover gives $h \in \ker\psi$ with $h \ge \delta > 0$, so $0 = \psi(h) \ge \delta$, which is absurd. So $\ker\psi \subseteq \ker \mathrm{ev}_x$ for some $x$, the two hyperplanes agree, and $\psi = \mathrm{ev}_x$.

steps.slogan: Show that $C$ is a fully faithful functor into the unital spaces.
steps.detail: For continuous $g\colon Y \to X$, the map $f \mapsto f \circ g$ is a unital Riesz homomorphism $C(X) \to C(Y)$, and $C(X)$ is Archimedean and complete in the sup norm. Conversely a unital Riesz homomorphism $\Phi$ gives, for each $y$, the character $\mathrm{ev}_y \circ \Phi = \mathrm{ev}_{g(y)}$, where $g$ is continuous because $X$ has the weak topology of $C(X)$. So $\Phi = C(g)$ for a unique $g$.

steps.slogan: Make the unital Riesz homomorphisms of $E$ a compact Hausdorff space.
steps.detail: Each unital Riesz homomorphism $\phi$ has $|\phi(x)| \le \|x\|$, so $X_E$ is a closed subset of $\prod_x [-\|x\|, \|x\|]$, compact by Tychonoff's theorem and Hausdorff. The evaluation $\hat{x}(\phi) = \phi(x)$ is continuous, and $x \mapsto \hat{x}$ is a unital Riesz homomorphism $E \to C(X_E)$.

steps.slogan: Find a unital Riesz homomorphism that is large at a given positive element.
steps.detail: Let $x > 0$ and pick $\varepsilon > 0$ with $x \not\le \varepsilon u$ (Archimedean). The ideal generated by $(\varepsilon u - x)^+$ misses the disjoint element $(x - \varepsilon u)^+ \ne 0$, so it omits $u$. A maximal proper ideal $M$ above it exists by Zorn; $E/M$ is simple, hence totally ordered and Archimedean, so it is $\mathbb R$, and the quotient map $\phi$ has $\phi(x) \ge \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Show that evaluation is an isometry onto $C(X_E)$ by Stone-Weierstrass.
steps.detail: For $x \ge 0$ with $\|x\| = 1$ and each $\varepsilon < 1$, step 4 gives $\phi_\varepsilon$ with $\phi_\varepsilon(x) \ge \varepsilon$; a cluster point in the compact $X_E$ has value $1$ at $x$. So evaluation is injective and isometric, and its image is a closed vector sublattice with $1$ that separates points of $X_E$. By Stone-Weierstrass it is dense, hence all of $C(X_E)$.

steps.slogan: Combine full faithfulness and essential surjectivity into the dual equivalence.
steps.detail: By step 2 the functor $C$ is fully faithful, and by step 5 every object $(E, u)$ is isomorphic to $C(X_E)$ through $x \mapsto \hat{x}$. So $C$ is a dual equivalence, with inverse $E \mapsto X_E$.

concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compact Hausdorff spaces are the objects on one side of the duality.
concepts.c:riesz-space: Archimedean Riesz spaces with unit are the objects on the other side.

source.note: Yosida's representation theorem (1941); the norm-complete case is due to Kakutani (1941). Westerbaan, Yosida Duality, arXiv:1612.03327, gives the categorical form.

statement: A set $E \subseteq \mathbb R$ is the set of points of [non-differentiability](c:non-differentiability) of some [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ if and only if $E = A \cup B$, where $A$ is a [G-delta set](c:g-delta-subspace) and $B$ is a $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set of [measure zero](c:measure-zero).

hypotheses.text: $E$ is a subset of $\mathbb R$.

conclusion: $E$ is the non-differentiability set of a continuous function exactly when it is the union of a $G_\delta$ set and a null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set.

proofs.name: Dini derivates and two constructions
proofs.slogan: Split the non-differentiability set by infinite Dini derivates to prove necessity, and add two constructed functions to prove sufficiency.
proofs.scope: Both directions; the two constructions in steps 3 and 4 are long and rest on the cited papers. Here differentiable means a finite derivative.

roles.why: The set $E$ is split into a $G_\delta$ part and a disjoint null part in the sufficiency direction.

steps.slogan: Split a [non-differentiability](c:non-differentiability) set into a $G_\delta$ set and a null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set.
steps.detail: For continuous $f$ the differentiability set is $F_{\sigma\delta}$ (Cauchy criterion on rational increments), so $N_f$ is $G_{\delta\sigma}$. The set $G$ where some Dini derivate is infinite is a finite union of $G_\delta$ sets inside $N_f$. By the Denjoy-Young-Saks theorem, almost every point with all four derivates finite is a point of differentiability, so $N_f \setminus G$ is a null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set.

steps.slogan: Reduce sufficiency to a $G_\delta$ set and a disjoint null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set.
steps.detail: Given $E = A \cup B$, replace $B$ by $B' = B \setminus A$. Then $B'$ is still a null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set, because $\mathbb R \setminus A$ is $F_\sigma$, and $E = A \sqcup B'$.

steps.slogan: Build a continuous function that is non-differentiable exactly on a null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set.
steps.detail: Zahorski constructs, for every null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set $B'$, a continuous function $f_1$ with $N_{f_1} = B'$. Fowler and Preiss give a simpler proof, with $f_1$ Lipschitz.

steps.slogan: Build a continuous function that is non-differentiable exactly on a given $G_\delta$ set.
steps.detail: The cited paper constructs, for every $G_\delta$ set $A$, a continuous function $f_2$ with $N_{f_2} = A$. This is the long part of that paper.

steps.slogan: Add the two functions to realize the union.
steps.detail: Let $f = f_1 + f_2$. At a point of $B'$ the function $f_2$ is differentiable and $f_1$ is not; at a point of $A$ the function $f_1$ is differentiable and $f_2$ is not; elsewhere both are differentiable. So $N_f = A \sqcup B' = E$.

steps.slogan: Combine necessity and sufficiency into the characterization.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that every non-differentiability set is a union of a $G_\delta$ set and a null $G_{\delta\sigma}$ set. Steps 2 to 5 show that every such union is a non-differentiability set.

concepts.c:non-differentiability: The theorem describes the set of points where a function is not differentiable.
concepts.c:continuous-function: The function class is continuous functions on the real line.
concepts.c:g-delta-subspace: $G_\delta$ sets are one of the two classes in the description.
concepts.c:measure-zero: The second class consists of null sets.

source.ref: Z. Zahorski, Sur l'ensemble des points de non-derivabilite d'une fonction continue, Bulletin de la Societe Mathematique de France 74 (1946), 147-178
source.note: Steps 1 and 2 and 5 are short arguments; steps 3 and 4 are Zahorski's constructions. Fowler and Preiss, A simple proof of Zahorski's description of non-differentiability sets of Lipschitz functions, Real Analysis Exchange 34 (2009), 127-138, simplify step 3.

statement: Let $f \not\equiv 0$ be an [entire function](c:entire-function) of [exponential type](c:function-of-exponential-type) $\tau$ with $f(x) \ge 0$ for real $x$, and let $z_n$ be its zeros. Then $f = F F^*$, with $F$ entire of exponential type $\tau/2$ and all zeros in the closed upper half plane and $F^*(z) = \overline{F(\bar z)}$, if and only if $\sum_n |\operatorname{Im}(1/z_n)| < \infty$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f \not\equiv 0$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function) of [exponential type](c:function-of-exponential-type) $\tau$.
The function $f$ is nonnegative on the real axis.

conclusion: A factorization $f = F F^*$ with $F$ of type $\tau/2$ and zeros in the closed upper half plane exists if and only if $\sum_n |\operatorname{Im}(1/z_n)| < \infty$.

proofs.name: Half product of the zeros
proofs.slogan: Pair the zeros by conjugation, bound them by Lindelof's theorem for one direction, and build the half product for the other.
proofs.scope: Both directions of the equivalence, with the facts of the Cartwright class taken from the literature. The outline rests on the cited work for steps 2 to 5.

roles.why: Exponential type gives Lindelof's bound on the zero sums and the indicator theory used for the type of $F$.
Nonnegativity makes $f$ real on $\mathbb R$, so zeros pair by conjugation and the constant in the factorization is positive.

steps.slogan: Show that the zeros of $f$ are symmetric about the real axis.
steps.detail: Since $f$ is real on $\mathbb R$, the reflection principle gives $f(z) = \overline{f(\bar z)}$, so the zeros come in conjugate pairs. A real zero of a nonnegative function has even multiplicity. So the zeros of $f$ are $w_n$ and $\bar w_n$ with all $w_n$ in the closed upper half plane.

steps.slogan: Bound the zero sums of $F$ by Lindelof's theorem to prove the forward direction.
steps.detail: If $f = F F^*$, the zeros $w_n$ of $F$ lie in the closed upper half plane. For an entire function of exponential type, the sums $\sum_{|w_n| < r} 1/w_n$ stay bounded (Lindelof), and all $\operatorname{Im}(1/w_n)$ have one sign, so $\sum |\operatorname{Im}(1/w_n)| < \infty$, and the same holds for the zeros of $f$.

steps.slogan: Build the half product $P$ over the zeros in the upper half plane.
steps.detail: Assume $\sum |\operatorname{Im}(1/z_n)| < \infty$. By the Cartwright-Levinson theory, $f$ is in the Cartwright class and the real parts of the zero sums converge too. So $P(z) = \lim_{R \to \infty} \prod_{|w_n| < R} (1 - z/w_n)$ converges to an entire function with zeros $w_n$.

steps.slogan: Factor $f$ as a positive constant times $P P^*$.
steps.detail: The functions $f$ and $P P^*$ have the same zeros and both lie in the Cartwright class, so $f = c\, e^{ibz} P P^*$ with $b$ real. On $\mathbb R$ we have $P P^* = |P|^2 \ge 0$ and $f \ge 0$, so $b = 0$ and $c > 0$.

steps.slogan: Multiply by $e^{icz}$ to give $F$ the exponential type $\tau/2$.
steps.detail: For $F = \sqrt{c}\, e^{icz} P$ with real $c$, the product $F F^*$ is unchanged. The indicators of $F$ and $F^*$ add up to that of $f$, so $h_F(\pi/2) + h_F(-\pi/2) = \tau$. The factor $e^{icz}$ moves the two values in opposite directions, so a choice of $c$ makes both equal to $\tau/2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 2 proves that a factorization with $F$ of type $\tau/2$ and zeros in the closed upper half plane forces $\sum |\operatorname{Im}(1/z_n)| < \infty$. Steps 3 to 5 prove the converse.

concepts.c:entire-function: The theorem factors an entire function.
concepts.c:function-of-exponential-type: Exponential type controls the zero sums and the indicator of $F$.

source.ref: N. I. Akhiezer, On the theory of entire functions of finite degree, Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR 63 (1948), 475-478
source.note: The facts on the Cartwright class (Lindelof, Cartwright-Levinson, indicators) are in B. Ya. Levin, Distribution of Zeros of Entire Functions, American Mathematical Society, 1964 (revised 1980).

statement: Let $f, \varphi$ be real functions on $[a, b]$ with the smoothness and scale conditions below, and let $f'(x_\mu) = \mu$. Then the [trigonometric sum](c:exponential-sum) $\sum_{a < n \le b} \varphi(n) e^{2\pi i f(n)}$ equals a shorter sum of stationary-phase terms, one for each $\mu$ between $f'(a)$ and $f'(b)$, plus an explicit remainder.

hypotheses.text: The functions $f^{(4)}$ and $\varphi''$ are continuous on $[a, b]$.
For some $H > 0$ and $1 \ll U \ll V$ with $0 < b - a \le V$: $f'' \asymp 1/U$, $|f'''| \ll 1/(UV)$, $|f^{(4)}| \ll 1/(UV^2)$, $|\varphi| \ll H$, $|\varphi'| \ll H/V$, $|\varphi''| \ll H/V^2$.

conclusion: With $\alpha = f'(a)$ and $\beta = f'(b)$, the sum equals $\sum_{\alpha \le \mu \le \beta} C(\mu) Z(\mu) + R$, where $Z(\mu) = \varphi(x_\mu)\, e^{2\pi i (f(x_\mu) - \mu x_\mu + 1/8)} / \sqrt{f''(x_\mu)}$, $C(\mu) = 1$ for $\alpha < \mu < \beta$, $C(\alpha) = C(\beta) = \frac12$, and $R \ll H(\log(\beta - \alpha + 2) + T_a + T_b)$ with boundary terms $T_a, T_b$ defined in the source.

proofs.name: Poisson summation and stationary phase
proofs.slogan: Write the sum as a sum of oscillatory integrals by Poisson summation and evaluate each integral by stationary phase.
proofs.scope: Outline of the Karatsuba-Korolev proof; the exact remainder $R$ and the boundary terms $T_a, T_b$ are defined in the cited paper. The estimates of steps 3 and 4 rest on that paper.

roles.why: The continuous fourth and second derivatives allow the expansions with explicit error terms.
The derivative bounds make $f'$ increasing at a controlled rate and keep every error term of size $H$ times a small factor.

steps.slogan: Replace the sum by a sum of integrals with the Poisson summation formula.
steps.detail: Poisson summation gives $\sum_{a < n \le b} \varphi(n) e(f(n)) = \sum_{\mu \in \mathbb Z} \int_a^b \varphi(x) e(f(x) - \mu x)\,dx$, with weight $\frac12$ at an integer endpoint, up to the usual boundary corrections. Here $e(t) = e^{2\pi i t}$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate each integral with $\alpha < \mu < \beta$ by [stationary phase](c:stationary-phase).
steps.detail: For $\alpha < \mu < \beta$ the phase $f(x) - \mu x$ has the unique stationary point $x_\mu$, since $f'$ is strictly increasing. Stationary phase gives the term $Z(\mu)$, with an error controlled by the bounds on $f''', f^{(4)}, \varphi', \varphi''$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integrals with $\mu$ outside $[\alpha, \beta]$ by integration by parts.
steps.detail: Without a stationary point, integration by parts bounds each integral by boundary terms of size about $H/|\mu - \alpha|$ or $H/|\mu - \beta|$. Summing over $\mu$ gives the logarithmic term of $R$.

steps.slogan: Treat the integrals with $\mu$ near $\alpha$ or $\beta$ separately.
steps.detail: For such $\mu$ the stationary point lies near $a$ or $b$, and the endpoint contributions form the boundary terms $T_a$ and $T_b$ of $R$.

steps.slogan: Collect the main terms and the remainders into the stated formula.
steps.detail: The integrals with $\alpha \le \mu \le \beta$ give $\sum C(\mu) Z(\mu)$, with $C = \frac12$ at the endpoints from the half weights of Poisson summation. All other contributions add up to $R$.

concepts.c:exponential-sum: The theorem approximates this kind of sum.

source.ref: A. A. Karatsuba and M. A. Korolev, A theorem on the approximation of a trigonometric sum by a shorter one, Izvestiya Rossiiskoi Akademii Nauk, Seriya Matematicheskaya 71 (2007), no. 2, 123-150
source.note: Karatsuba proved the theorem in the 1980s without explicit constants; Karatsuba and Korolev computed the constants in the remainder.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group), $p$ a prime, $k$ an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$, and $D$ a $p$-subgroup of $G$. Then the Brauer correspondence is a bijection from the $p$-[blocks](c:block) of $G$ with defect group $D$ to the $p$-blocks of the [normalizer](c:normalizer) $N_G(D)$ with defect group $D$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $D$ is a $p$-subgroup of $G$.
$k$ is an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$.

conclusion: Block induction $b \mapsto b^G$ is a bijection from the blocks of $N_G(D)$ with defect group $D$ onto the blocks of $G$ with defect group $D$.

proofs.name: Brauer homomorphism and block induction
proofs.slogan: Use the Brauer homomorphism to induce blocks from the normalizer and to recover each block of defect group $D$ uniquely.
proofs.scope: The first main theorem. The second and third main theorems, on character values and generalized decomposition numbers, are the other members of the family and are not proved here; steps 3 and 4 rest on the cited work.

roles.why: The $p$-subgroup $D$ defines the Brauer homomorphism, and $N_G(D)$ is the group where blocks are induced from.
Algebraic closure and characteristic $p$ give the block idempotents and central characters used throughout.

steps.slogan: Define the Brauer homomorphism for the $p$-subgroup $D$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathrm{Br}_D\colon (kG)^D \to kC_G(D)$ project onto the span of the elements of $C_G(D)$. It is an algebra homomorphism on the $D$-fixed points of $kG$, and it maps $Z(kG)$ into $Z(kN_G(D))$.

steps.slogan: Describe defect groups of a block through the Brauer homomorphism.
steps.detail: For a block $B$ with idempotent $e_B \in Z(kG)$, a defect group is a maximal $p$-subgroup $P$ with $\mathrm{Br}_P(e_B) \ne 0$, and defect groups form one conjugacy class. So $B$ has defect group $D$ exactly when $D$ is maximal with $\mathrm{Br}_D(e_B) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Define block induction from $N_G(D)$ to $G$ through central characters.
steps.detail: For a block $b$ of $N_G(D)$ with central character $\omega_b$, Brauer's block induction gives the block $b^G$ of $G$ with $\omega_{b^G}(a) = \omega_b(\mathrm{Br}_D(a))$ for $a \in Z(kG)$. The map $b \mapsto b^G$ is the Brauer correspondence.

steps.slogan: Show that induction keeps the defect group $D$ and hits each block exactly once.
steps.detail: The cited work proves that $b^G$ has defect group $D$ if $b$ does. It also proves that, for $B$ with defect group $D$, exactly one block $b$ of $N_G(D)$ with defect group $D$ has $e_b\,\mathrm{Br}_D(e_B) \ne 0$, and that this $b$ satisfies $b^G = B$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that induction is a bijection with the stated inverse.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives a map from blocks of $G$ with defect group $D$ to blocks of $N_G(D)$ with defect group $D$, sending $B$ to the unique $b$ above. It is inverse to $b \mapsto b^G$, so the Brauer correspondence is a bijection.

concepts.c:finite-group: The theorem is about the blocks of a finite group.
concepts.c:block: Blocks of the group algebra are the objects put in bijection.
concepts.c:normalizer: The normalizer $N_G(D)$ is the local subgroup whose blocks correspond.

source.ref: G. Navarro, Characters and Blocks of Finite Groups, London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series 250, Cambridge University Press, 1998, Chapter 4 (Theorem 4.17)
source.note: Brauer's first main theorem is Theorem 4.17 of Navarro; steps 1 to 3 are the setup of that chapter.
